claim: OPA is an open source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack; it decouples policy decision-making from enforcement, taking JSON input plus policy (Rego) plus data and returning a decision. Documented deployment: server daemon, embedded Go library, REPL.
notes: Docs enumerate use cases (microservice authz, Kubernetes admission, CI/CD, API gateways). No domain objects for promotions, identity verification, ledgers, or approval workflows exist anywhere in the docs; used as architectural absence evidence for A/E/F and workflow squares.

claim: OPA graduated from CNCF on 2021-02-04. At graduation: user survey of 150+ organizations, 91% using OPA from QA to production; production users named include Goldman Sachs, Netflix, Pinterest, T-Mobile; maintainers spanned Google, Microsoft, VMware, Styra.
page_title: CNCF Announces Open Policy Agent Graduation
notes: CNCF is the project's governing foundation. Also supports free/self-serve distribution (Apache-2.0).

claim: Homepage positions OPA as 'a policy engine that streamlines policy management across your stack for improved development, security and audit capability'; shows a Rego example evaluating account state, risk scoring and transaction limits; displays adopter logos (Atlassian, Goldman Sachs, Capital One, Cisco, Intuit); links an interactive Play environment (Rego Playground).
notes: Homepage example is a risk/limits decision, showing intended fit for risk-style rule evaluation on provided attributes (not signal generation).

claim: Rego is a declarative, Datalog-inspired policy language: packages/modules, complete and partial rules, default/else, comprehensions, some/every quantifiers, user functions; extensive built-ins including time functions (time.now_ns, time.weekday), string ops, regex, io.jwt.* (JWT verify/decode), and http.send for external calls; JSON Schema based type checking; YAML metadata annotations on packages/rules including title, description, authors, related_resources, and custom key-value data.
page_title: Policy Language - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Metadata annotations (related_resources/custom) are the documented mechanism usable for legal-source provenance annotation; time built-ins enable temporal/effective-date logic written by the policy author.

claim: OPA decisions are not restricted to boolean allow/deny: 'OPA returns policy decisions - which can be simple yes/no answers or complex structured outputs', evaluated against arbitrary JSON input supplied by the caller.
notes: Allow/deny/review triage and reason codes are expressible as structured output, but the semantics must be authored per policy; there is no opinionated built-in tri-state decision model.

claim: Documented integration modes: REST API (daemon/sidecar; 'Running OPA locally on the same host as your application or service helps ensure policy decisions are fast and highly-available'), Go SDK (sdk.New/Decision with config, bundle management, decision logging), low-level Go rego package, WebAssembly compilation of policies for any language with a Wasm runtime, and Intermediate Representation (IR) plans; comparison table: REST fast / Go library faster / Wasm fastest.
page_title: Integrating OPA - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Supports B02/B03/H02: synchronous in-process or same-host evaluation is the documented pattern for production decisioning.

claim: Performance docs state OPA serves microservice API authorization decisions within 'a budget in the order of 1 millisecond'; describe the near-constant-time 'linear fragment', automatic rule indexing, early exit, comprehension indexing, partial-evaluation optimization levels (-O=1/-O=2), expression-level profiling (opa eval --profile) and benchmarking (opa bench, opa test --bench with p50/p90/p99 histograms).
page_title: Policy Performance - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Strongest official latency statement; corroborated by adopter-scale evidence (OPA-021 Pinterest).

claim: Data replicated into OPA is held in memory: raw JSON consumes approximately 20x more memory than serialized form (8MB JSON -> ~160MB); ~10,000 rules ~130MB, ~100,000 rules ~1.1GB; docs advise GOMEMLIMIT below container limits and disk storage for very large datasets.
page_title: Policy Performance - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Bounds how much customer/user context can practically live inside a vanilla OPA instance.

claim: Bundles are gzipped tarballs of policies and data downloaded by OPA via periodic polling with ETag caching (304 Not Modified) or HTTP long polling; the manifest carries a 'revision' identifier (typically a git commit hash or semver), 'roots' for namespace ownership across multiple bundles, and 'rego_version'; bundles can be persisted to disk for restart recovery; common distribution backends include S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Nginx and OCI registries.
notes: Revision metadata is the version link recorded in decision logs; storage/history of past bundle versions is the bundle server's or git's job, not OPA's.

claim: Bundles support cryptographic signing: .signatures.json contains JWTs over per-file SHA checksums; OPA verifies signature, payload-file match, and file hashes before activating a bundle, otherwise it keeps the existing bundle and reports activation failure via the Status API. Delta bundles (JSON Patch data updates) do not support signature verification.
notes: Integrity protection covers policy distribution; there is no equivalent signing/hash-chaining for emitted decision logs.

claim: Decision log events include: decision_id ('unique identifier generated for each decision for traceability'), input, result, path, bundles with revision metadata, RFC3339 timestamp, performance metrics, nd_builtin_cache (non-deterministic builtin inputs/outputs), W3C trace_id/span_id, requested_by, and instance labels; events are POSTed as gzip-compressed JSON arrays to a configurable remote service; console logging of decisions is also available.
page_title: Decision Logs - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Core evidence for D01-D04 and the raw material for reconstruction/replay; OPA ships no storage, query, or replay tooling for these events.

claim: Decision log masking: OPA queries data.system.log.mask to erase or upsert fields (JSON Pointers under /input, /result, /nd_builtin_cache) before upload; modifications are recorded in 'erased' and 'masked' event fields.
page_title: Decision Logs - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Policy-driven redaction supports PII handling in decision evidence.

claim: Decision log delivery uses adaptive buffering against upload_size_limit_bytes; max_decisions_per_second drops excess events when exceeded; oversized nd_builtin_cache fields are dropped to preserve the event. OPA provides no long-term retention: storage and retention are the responsibility of the receiving service.
page_title: Decision Logs - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: Retention controls (D08) and completeness guarantees are explicitly delegated to the sink; events can be dropped under load by configuration.

claim: Status API: OPA POSTs status reports to a remote endpoint (/status[/<partition>]) whenever bundles are downloaded/activated or plugin state changes; reports contain per-bundle name, active revision, request/download/activation timestamps, error details including parse/compile errors on failed activation, bundle size/type, plugin states, decision-log upload metrics, and instance labels; Prometheus exposure is available.
notes: This is the rollout-health half of change management: operators can observe which policy revision is live on which instance and detect failed activations.

claim: Discovery: OPA instances periodically download a discovery bundle whose JSON or Rego content generates each instance's configuration (which bundles to pull, decision log and status destinations, signing keys), enabling one control plane to serve differently-configured fleets keyed on labels/environment; the discovery section itself and service references are immutable to prevent lockout.
notes: Agent-side fleet management primitives exist; the server side (authoring, review, storage, UI) must be built or sourced separately.

claim: REST API: Data API GET/POST /v1/data/{path} evaluates policies with JSON input; query params include metrics, explain (notes/fails/full/debug) and provenance (returns OPA version and bundle revisions with the response); responses carry result and decision_id; Policy API provides CRUD over policy modules; Query API for ad hoc queries; Compile API POST /v1/compile for partial evaluation and /v1/compile/{path} for SQL/UCAST data filters; health endpoints (/health, /health/live, /health/ready with policy-based checks); bearer-token authentication via --authentication=token.
page_title: REST API - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: v0/v1 path versioning visible in API surface. Policy evaluation is read-only/side-effect-free; the Policy/Data write APIs are configuration-style, with no transactional or idempotency-key machinery documented.

claim: Policy testing: opa test runs test_-prefixed Rego rules; 'with' keyword mocks input, data and functions; --coverage reports evaluated/unevaluated lines; opa test --bench benchmarks tests (gobench format); data-driven/parameterized tests supported; --fail-on-empty for CI; --run regex filtering; --var-values diagnostics.
page_title: Policy Testing - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: First-class offline simulation/unit-testing of policies; no built-in what-if analysis against production traffic in OPA itself (that was EOPA LIA, see OPA-025).

claim: Documented external-data patterns: (1) JWT claims (stale until re-auth, size-limited), (2) input overloading by the calling service, (3) bundle replication ('OPA stores the entire datasource at once in memory'; staleness = replication lag + polling interval; 'policy and its corresponding data always arrive at the same time'), (4) push data into OPA's API with delta updates, (5) pull during evaluation via http.send ('External data is perfectly fresh' but 'Latency and availability of decision-making are dependent on the network').
page_title: External Data - Open Policy Agent Documentation
notes: OPA consumes whatever signals integrators supply; there are no vendor connectors, no schema normalization, and no signal-generation capability. http.send is the only generic third-party call-out path.

claim: Philosophy doc: policies 'encode important knowledge' about compliance; decoupling lets policy owners 'read, write, analyze, version, distribute, and in general manage policy separate from the service itself', and 'increases the consistency of policy compliance, and mitigates the risk of human error'; policies should be 'updated at any time without recompiling or redeploying'.
notes: OPA's stated purpose is exactly the substrate role for executable organizational/compliance rules; it stops at the substrate (no regulatory content, roles, or workflow).

claim: Monitoring: Prometheus /metrics endpoint enabled by default (Go runtime + HTTP latency histograms; status-plugin bundle load/activation metrics); OpenTelemetry distributed tracing emits a span per REST request with an opa.decision_id attribute when decision logging is active, plus descendant spans for http.send calls; /health APIs.
notes: Observability is production-grade and standards-based (Prometheus/OTel).

claim: ADOPTERS.md production users: Goldman Sachs (K8s admission + RBAC provisioning), Netflix (access control across microservices using contextual data from remote resources), Intuit (~50 clusters), Pinterest (Kafka/Envoy/Jenkins policy; ~400K QPS Kafka authorization without caching, ~8.5M QPS with caching), T-Mobile, BNY Mellon (sidecar authz using Active Directory context), Capital One (admission control), State Street, Atlassian (microservice API authorization, policies distributed via S3), Appsflyer (hundreds of microservices delegate authorization to central OPA incorporating data privacy regulations and consent policies), Cloudflare.
notes: Appsflyer is direct evidence of regulatory-domain (privacy/consent) policy running on OPA; heavy regulated-industry adoption (GS, Capital One, BNY Mellon, State Street) for infrastructure/authorization policy.

claim: 2025-08-20 project announcement: OPA creators (Teemu Koponen, Tim Hinrichs, Torin Sandall) and several Styra engineers joined Apple; 'Open Policy Agent remains a CNCF graduated open source project and there are no changes to the project governance or licensing'; Enterprise OPA (EOPA), OPA Control Plane, Regal, and multiple SDKs (TypeScript, React, C#, Java and others) move to the CNCF OPA GitHub organization; roadmap continues with monthly releases.
page_title: Note from Teemu, Tim, and Torin to the OPA Community - OPA Blog
notes: Definitive first-party account of the Styra->Apple transition and disposition of the commercial tooling.

claim: Styra (the company commercializing OPA via Styra DAS) has effectively wound down: third-party analysis describes an acqui-hire by Apple, prospective customers unable to reach Styra sales, and customer access to the DAS SaaS platform expected to disappear 'within the next 12 months' of the Aug-2025 announcement; styra.com and docs.styra.com were unreachable (DNS/connection timeouts) when checked on 2026-08-18.
page_title: OPA Announcement & Consequences - PAC Labs (John Brothers)
notes: Corroborated by Oso's post (OPA-036) and news coverage (BigGo/heise via search); direct fetch attempts to styra.com and docs.styra.com timed out twice each on access date, consistent with a shut-down web presence. No official Styra statement retrievable.

claim: Enterprise OPA (EOPA) — 'a version of OPA designed for data heavy workloads, with data-filtering functionality included', with data-source integrations (DynamoDB, Postgres, Neo4j) — was donated to the open-policy-agent GitHub organization under Apache-2.0, then archived on 2026-06-26 (read-only); maintainers invite community use ('mix and match your own OPA+') and are seeking new maintainers.
notes: The enterprise-grade OPA distribution currently has no active maintainer: its differentiating features are available as code but unsupported.

claim: Live Impact Analysis (LIA) was an Enterprise OPA feature that previewed the impact of policy changes before deployment by sampling live production traffic and comparing results of the new policy against the currently deployed policy, triggered from the CLI; positioned to 'catch any production-impacting changes early in the policy lifecycle, before they go live'.
page_title: Testing policy updates with Live Impact Analysis - Styra Documentation
notes: docs.styra.com unreachable on access date; content corroborated via search snippets and Styra marketing pages. Feature lives in the now-archived EOPA codebase, not in OPA proper — impact analysis against live traffic is NOT a vanilla-OPA capability.

claim: OPA Control Plane (OCP, open-policy-agent/opa-control-plane) is an Apache-2.0 open-source management system: builds bundles from Rego across multiple Git repositories with 'native environment promotion via Git workflows', build-time fetching/bundling of external HTTP datasources, bundle distribution to S3/GCS/Azure Blob, and hierarchical org-wide rules with label-based selection and Rego-based conflict resolution; active development (~798 commits) but early adoption (65 stars) and includes an opactl CLI.
notes: The community successor to the control-plane role Styra DAS played; git-based, headless, no approval-workflow UI, early maturity relative to DAS.

claim: Regal is 'a linter, debugger and language server for Rego' (Apache-2.0, now under the open-policy-agent org): rule categories for bugs/idiomatic/imports/performance/style/testing plus custom organizational rules; language-server integrations (VS Code, Neovim, Zed, Helix), Debug Adapter Protocol support, CI/pre-commit integration; in beta toward 1.0; users cited include Atlassian, Boeing, Miro.
notes: Policy-authoring quality tooling; supports custom organizational policy-style enforcement.

claim: OPA remains actively maintained post-transition: v1.19.1 released 2026-08-17 (Go security update), v1.19.0 on 2026-07-30 (SQL-injection fixes in data filters, stricter safety checks, Wasm runtime improvements, new built-in), v1.18.2 on 2026-07-02; roughly monthly release cadence.
notes: Counters concern that the Apple move stalled the OSS project: release the day before access date.

claim: OPA 1.0 was released 2024-12-20 ('A New Standard for Policy as Code') after ~10 years and 450+ contributors, making Rego v1 (if/contains keywords, strict-mode requirements) the default; bundles carry a rego_version field (0 or 1) for compatibility.
notes: Language/API stability signal relevant to enterprise adoption and versioning.

claim: The official ecosystem page catalogs: language SDK integrations (JavaScript, Java, C#, Go, Swift, Clojure, Rust, PHP, Zig); control planes / management products built on OPA — Styra, Permit.io, Aserto, Topaz, OPAL ('Open Policy Administration Layer'); application authorization integrations (Envoy, Spring Security, Kafka topic authorization, APISIX, Traefik, Pomerium); Kubernetes (OPA Gatekeeper 'Rego Policy Controller for Kubernetes'); Terraform/IaC integrations (Spacelift, Scalr, CloudFormation hooks).
notes: The catalog contains infrastructure/authorization integrations only — no legal, regulatory, promotions, identity-verification, or ledger entries; used as enumerated-absence evidence for C06/C10/E/F scores.

claim: The project's Support page lists only two third-party commercial support vendors — Policy-as-Code Laboratories (strategy/integration consulting for OPA and Rego) and DepKeep (enterprise open-source support/maintenance/security fixes) — with the disclaimer 'This list is not vetted by the OPA project maintainers and inclusion is not an endorsement'; the project itself offers no SLA.
notes: Positive evidence for the absence of vendor SLAs and first-party professional services after Styra's wind-down.

claim: OPA project security posture: third-party security audit by Cure53 (report public), documented vulnerability disclosure process (open-policy-agent-security@googlegroups.com, SECURITY.md); repository at 12.1k stars, Apache-2.0.
notes: Project-level assurance only; SOC 2-style service attestations are inapplicable because OPA is self-hosted software, so deployment compliance burden falls on the adopter.

claim: OPA's own APIs are secured via TLS (cert/key flags with auto-reload), authentication by bearer token (--authentication=token) or client TLS certificates (--authentication=tls), and authorization by a Rego policy at data.system.authz.allow (--authorization=basic) receiving identity, method, path, params, headers and body — enabling restrictions such as limiting which tokens may update policies vs query decisions.
notes: Access control over OPA is itself policy-coded; there are no user accounts, roles, directories, or SSO/SAML — identity is whatever token/cert the operator provisions.

claim: Swift OPA (announced 2025-05-14) enables native in-process policy evaluation in Swift applications using OPA's Intermediate Representation format.
notes: Example of the widening multi-language embedded-evaluation story (alongside Go, Wasm, donated Java/TS/C# SDKs).

claim: OpenFGA is 'an open-source authorization solution' implementing relationship-based access control (ReBAC) 'from the best ideas from Google's Zanzibar paper', maintained as a CNCF incubating project, with millisecond-scale checks and multi-language SDKs — an adjacent substitute for application authorization workloads.
notes: Adjacent competitor discovery: stateful relationship-graph authorization vs OPA's stateless rule evaluation.

claim: Oso (osohq.com) analysis (2025-08-20, updated 2025-09-09): Apple's hire of core OPA maintainers is an acqui-hire; Styra's enterprise offerings like DAS 'will no longer receive active development' and 'organizations should not expect the same commercial roadmap or enterprise-level support'; Oso positions its Polar-language, application-authorization product as a commercially supported alternative.
page_title: OPA maintainers join Apple; OSS community to maintain Styra Products - Oso
notes: Competitor commentary — discount positioning claims; used for DAS status corroboration and as an adjacent competitor discovery (Oso).
